title: The Planet Without a Visa: from Yanovka to the Study at Coyoacan
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Yanovka and the Schools of the South

stops.name: Yanovka, the birth on the grain estate
stops.date_confidence: attested. 7 November 1879 New Style, 26 October Old Style. The place is the hamlet of Yanovka in Kherson governorate, now Bereslavka, Ukraine.
stops.campa: On a grain estate in the open steppe of Kherson governorate, far from any town, Anna Bronstein bears a fifth child and he is named Lev Davidovich. His father David farms several hundred desyatinas and cannot read; the household is Jewish, prosperous, and speaks the mixed Russian and Ukrainian of the countryside. There is no politics in the house and no library in it either. Eight children are born here and half of them die young. Fifty years later, in Turkish exile, he will open the account of his own life by refusing the usual sentiment about childhood.
stops.quote: Childhood is looked upon as the happiest time of life. Is that always true? No, only a few have a happy childhood.
stops.quote_source: My Life: An Attempt at an Autobiography (1930), Chapter I, 'Yanovka'
suggested_refs: The Bronstein grain estate at Yanovka (Bereslavka), Kherson governorate
sources: Trotsky, My Life (1930), Chapter I, marxists.org

stops.name: Odessa, the Realschule of St Paul
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was sent to Odessa at about age eight to live with relatives and enrolled at the Lutheran German-language St Paul's Realschule, remaining until 1896. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The relative is usually named as Moisey Shpentzer, a printer and publisher; the name is standard in the literature and is not itemised in the verified pool.
stops.campa: At about eight he is taken off the steppe and sent to the city, to the household of a cousin of his mother who prints and publishes books, and enrolled at St Paul's Realschule, a Lutheran school where the teaching is in German and the pupils are Greeks, Germans, Poles and Jews in one room. Here the farm boy acquires the thing that outlasts every party he will ever join: a Russian prose style, exact and combative, learned in a house where books were made. He tops his class. He is also suspended for a season for leading his classmates against a teacher.
stops.quote: Mine was the grayish childhood of a lower-middle-class family, spent in a village in an obscure corner where nature is wide, and manners, views and interests are pinched and narrow.
stops.quote_source: My Life: An Attempt at an Autobiography (1930), Chapter I, 'Yanovka'
suggested_refs: St Paul's Realschule, Odessa, the Lutheran German-language school of his boyhood
sources: Trotsky, My Life (1930), Chapter I, marxists.org

stops.name: Nikolayev, the garden commune and the Workers' Union
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Nikolayev period, the conversion to Marxism and the founding of the South Russian Workers' Union. The sources conflict on the graduation year: the verified chronology as supplied dates the first-class honours and the brief Odessa University enrolment to 1897, while English Wikipedia gives honours in 1896 and the dropping out in early 1897. Both readings are recorded here and neither is adjudicated.
stops.campa: He is sent to Nikolayev to finish school and boards with a family whose sons are already radicals. In a garden on the edge of the town a circle of adolescents argues Marxism against populism night after night; Lev takes the populist side first, largely to win the argument, and is converted out of it by Aleksandra Sokolovskaya, older than him and better read. Within a year the debating circle has become the South Russian Workers' Union, with a hectographed paper and some two hundred members among the dock and mill hands of the port. He graduates with first-class honours and enrols at Odessa University to read mathematics, then leaves.
suggested_refs: The hectographed sheets of the South Russian Workers' Union, Nikolayev, 1897

segments.name: The Prisons and the First Siberia

stops.name: Nikolayev prison, the first arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrest in January 1898 with more than two hundred members of the union, and roughly two years of imprisonment at Nikolayev, Kherson, Odessa and Moscow before sentencing. The specific reading matter of the prison years comes from his own account and is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: In January the police take the union apart, arresting more than two hundred people, and Bronstein among them. He is nineteen. What follows is about two years of cells at Nikolayev, then Kherson, then Odessa, then Moscow, some of them without a single book and some of them with a whole prison library, and he uses them as he will use every enforced stillness of his life. He reads. Theology, the Gospels in four languages, the Italian rationalists, and finally Marx. He is moved from cell to cell for two years and the sentence is not handed down until 1900.
suggested_refs: The transit-prison chain of Nikolayev, Kherson, Odessa and Moscow, 1898-1900

stops.name: Moscow, the marriage in the transfer prison
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage to Aleksandra Sokolovskaya in a Moscow prison in July 1900 and the four-year Siberian sentence handed down the same year. The identification of the prison as Butyrka rests on Trotsky's own account of the Moscow transfer prison; the Butyrka article does not list him among its inmates. Coordinates are Butyrka's corrected position, 55.78444 N 37.59389 E; the pool as supplied gave 55.7864/37.5866, about five hundred metres off.
stops.campa: Awaiting sentence in the Moscow transfer prison, he marries Aleksandra Sokolovskaya, the woman who argued him out of populism in the Nikolayev garden. The ceremony is performed inside the walls, and its practical purpose is administrative: a married pair will be sent to the same place. The sentence handed down that year is four years of exile in Siberia. They travel east together as husband and wife, under escort. Of the union they were arrested for, eighteen months earlier, the two of them are what is left.
suggested_refs: The Moscow transfer prison, usually identified with Butyrka, site of the July 1900 marriage

stops.name: Ust-Kut, Antid Oto on the Lena
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Ust-Kut exile, the pen name Antid Oto, the work for Vostochnoye obozreniye and the birth of Zinaida in Siberian exile in 1901. Month and day of the birth unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates corrected to 56.783 N, 105.633 E; the pool as supplied gave 105.7833, about nine kilometres too far east.
stops.campa: The exile settlement sits on the upper Lena where the river is still narrow and the winter runs eight months. Here he writes for the Irkutsk paper Vostochnoye obozreniye under the pen name Antid Oto, and discovers that prose can be paid for: literary criticism, essays on Nietzsche and Ibsen, the beginnings of the manner that will make him the most readable Marxist writing in Russian. Their first daughter, Zinaida, is born in the settlement. Vostochnoye obozreniye is a legal paper in a censored empire, so everything he actually wants to say has to be said sideways.
suggested_refs: Vostochnoye obozreniye, Irkutsk, carrying the Antid Oto essays of 1901-1902

stops.name: Verkholensk, the second daughter and the decision to run
stops.date_confidence: attested that a second daughter, Nina, was born in Siberian exile in 1902 and that the escape followed in the summer of that year. Month and day of the birth unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates corrected to 54.10 N, 105.57 E per Russian Wikipedia; the pool as supplied gave 53.9667/105.05, roughly forty kilometres southwest of the settlement.
stops.campa: Moved to another Lena settlement, the family grows: a second daughter, Nina, is born in 1902. Exile in this form is not a camp. It is a village, a small state stipend, a police register to sign, and years of nothing, which is why so many of the exiled simply walk out of it. Bronstein walks out of it, leaving Sokolovskaya in the settlement with two daughters, the elder not yet two years old. The household ends here and the political friendship does not. What the two of them said to each other about that is not in any source reachable from this file.
suggested_refs: The Lena exile settlements of Ust-Kut and Verkholensk, Irkutsk governorate

stops.name: Irkutsk, the name written into the blank passport
stops.date_confidence: attested: escape from Siberian exile in the summer of 1902, concealed in a hay cart, travelling west on a false passport made out in the name Trotsky. That the name was taken from a head jailer at the Odessa prison rests on Trotsky's own account in My Life and has no independent confirmation; flagged [R]. Irkutsk is used here as a route pin on the westward journey, not as an attested overnight stop. Month set to June for ordering.
stops.campa: Friends hide him in a cart under a load of hay and drive him past the police posts while a dummy lies in his bed in the settlement. Somewhere on the road west a blank passport has to be filled in, and the name he writes into it is Trotsky. His own account, given nearly thirty years later, says it belonged to a head jailer at the Odessa prison where he had been held; nobody has confirmed that from any other direction. He means it for one journey. He signs it for the remaining thirty-eight years of his life.
suggested_refs: Trotsky, My Life (1930), on the origin of the name taken from an Odessa jailer
sources: Trotsky, My Life (1930), marxists.org (for the jailer account, uncorroborated)

segments.name: Iskra, the Split, and the Fifty Days

stops.name: London, Clerkenwell Green and the Iskra board
stops.date_confidence: attested that Trotsky reached London from Siberia in 1902, joined the circle around Iskra, was known by the byline Pero, and that Lenin proposed him for the editorial board over Plekhanov's objection. The scene of the arrival at Lenin's lodging comes from Trotsky's own memoir. Month set to October 1902 for ordering.
stops.campa: He arrives in London in the autumn and is taken straight to the room where Lenin is still asleep. The household already knows him by his byline: Pero, the Pen. Iskra is printed at Clerkenwell Green in the premises of a radical press and smuggled into Russia, and its board is split between the older emigration of Plekhanov and Zasulich and the younger of Lenin and Martov. Lenin proposes the twenty-three-year-old as a seventh editor. Plekhanov blocks it, correctly identifying whose vote the new man would be. Trotsky lectures to Russian emigres in Whitechapel for his supper.
suggested_refs: The Twentieth Century Press building at 37a Clerkenwell Green, where Iskra was printed

stops.name: Paris, Natalia Ivanovna Sedova
stops.date_confidence: attested that Trotsky met Natalia Sedova in 1902 shortly after the escape from Siberia and that they became partners in 1903, remaining together until his death. The sources give the location loosely as Western Europe; Paris is the usual placing and the canonical atlas Paris pin (48.8566, 2.3522) is inherited here. Month set to November 1902 for ordering.
stops.campa: Sent to lecture in Paris, he meets Natalia Ivanovna Sedova, an art historian working inside the same emigre network. She takes him through the Louvre; the only account of that afternoon is his own, and in it he argues with the paintings. They become partners the following year and remain so for thirty-seven, through Vienna, Petrograd, the Kremlin, Prinkipo, Norway and Coyoacan. Two sons are born inside the partnership, Lev and Sergei, and neither of them outlives his father. She is in the house on the last afternoon of his life and she survives him by twenty-two years.
suggested_refs: Natalia Sedova's own memoir material on the Paris meeting and the years that followed

stops.name: Brussels, the Second Congress in the flour warehouse
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Second Congress of the RSDLP opened in Brussels on 30 July 1903 (17 July Old Style) in a flour warehouse, and the delegates were forced out of Belgium on 6 August 1903 under Russian diplomatic pressure. The verified pool as supplied placed the congress in London throughout and a separate lens named the Maison du Peuple as the venue; both are corrected here. Coordinates are Brussels city centre, since the warehouse address is not established and the Maison du Peuple was demolished in 1965.
stops.campa: Delegates gather in a flea-ridden flour warehouse to found, properly, a Russian Social Democratic Labour Party that already has a newspaper and almost no organisation. They argue for three weeks about the first paragraph of the party rules, which is to say about who counts as a member: anyone who accepts the programme and gives the party regular help, or only those who take part personally in one of its organisations. Lenin wants the narrower formula. Trotsky, who came to London as Lenin's man, hears in it something he does not like, and says so on the floor. On the sixth of August the Belgian police put them all out of the country.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, '2nd Congress of the RSDLP', for the Brussels opening and the expulsion of 6 August 1903

stops.name: London, the congress reconvened and the party split
stops.date_confidence: attested: the congress reconvened in London after the expulsion of 6 August 1903 and closed there on 23 August 1903 (10 August Old Style), splitting into Bolshevik and Menshevik factions. Trotsky sided with the Mensheviks at the congress and formally left them in September 1904, thereafter calling himself a non-factional social democrat for over a decade.
stops.campa: The congress reassembles in London and finishes there on the twenty-third of August, having split the party it came to found. Lenin's side takes the name Bolshevik, majority, from a vote on the composition of the editorial board; Martov's takes Menshevik, minority, and carries the losing name for twenty years. Trotsky goes with Martov, against the man who brought him out of Siberia and into the board a year earlier. The question underneath is whether a party is an army. Lenin's answer is yes. Nobody leaving the hall thinks the split will hold.
suggested_refs: The minutes of the Second Congress of the RSDLP, London sessions, August 1903

stops.name: St Petersburg, chairman of the Soviet
stops.date_confidence: attested: clandestine return to Russia in February 1905 after Bloody Sunday, an address to a crowd estimated at 200,000 on 15 October 1905, election as chairman of the St Petersburg Soviet on 26 November 1905 after the arrest of Georgy Khrustalev-Nosar. Old and New Style are not distinguished in the supplied chronology and are not adjudicated here. The alias Yanovsky is given in the geography lens.
stops.campa: He comes back into Russia in February on a false passport, under the name Yanovsky, and by October the general strike has produced a body nobody designed: a council of workers' deputies elected off the factory benches, meeting in the capital while the government is still sitting. On the fifteenth of October he speaks to a crowd put at two hundred thousand. On the twenty-sixth of November, the chairman Khrustalev-Nosar having been arrested, the Soviet elects him in that man's place. He is twenty-six. The Soviet lasts fifty days in all.
suggested_refs: The minutes and proclamations of the St Petersburg Soviet of Workers' Deputies, October to December 1905

stops.name: Peter and Paul Fortress, the trial used as a platform
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Financial Manifesto of 2 December 1905, the arrest of the Soviet's leadership the following day, and conviction on 4 October 1906 for supporting armed rebellion with a sentence of perpetual Siberian exile and loss of civil rights. Lev Sedov's birth is corrected here to Saint Petersburg, 24 February 1906; the pool as supplied gave Vienna, which is chronologically impossible because Trotsky did not reach Vienna until October 1907.
stops.campa: On the second of December the Soviet issues a Financial Manifesto calling on Russia to stop paying taxes and to refuse to honour the government's foreign loans, and the police arrest its leadership the next day. He spends the following year in the fortress on the Neva, writing. In October 1906 he turns the trial into what he wanted from it, a public defence of armed insurrection printed in the newspapers and delivered by a defendant who denies nothing. The sentence is perpetual exile in Siberia with the loss of all civil rights. His son Lev is born in the city on the twenty-fourth of February that year, while his father is in a cell.
suggested_refs: The Financial Manifesto of the St Petersburg Soviet, 2 December 1905
sources: Russian Wikipedia, 'Sedov, Lev Lvovich' (for the corrected birthplace)

stops.name: Berezov, the escape by reindeer sledge
stops.date_confidence: attested: escape from Berezov in January 1907 while en route to permanent exile at Obdorsk, travelling by reindeer sledge and then by rail back to Europe. The feigned illness and the hired guide come from Trotsky's own narrative in My Life and are not independently confirmed; flagged [R] inside an otherwise attested escape. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The convoy is bound for Obdorsk above the Arctic Circle, more than a thousand versts from the nearest railway, and he does not intend to arrive. At Berezov he is left behind, ill, and from there he hires a driver and a reindeer sledge and crosses the frozen taiga westward until he reaches the Urals and a line of rail. It is his second escape from Siberia in five years. Both work for the same reason: the empire is enormous and cannot afford to watch its own distances.
suggested_refs: Trotsky's account of the Berezov escape, published as Tuda i obratno (There and Back)

segments.name: Vienna, the War, and the Planet Without a Visa

stops.name: Vienna, seven years and a second Pravda
stops.date_confidence: attested: settlement in Vienna from October 1907; the Russian-language Vienna Pravda from October 1908, edited with Adolph Joffe and Matvey Skobelev, folding in April 1912; Balkan War correspondence for Kievskaya Mysl; and the birth of Sergei Sedov in Vienna on 21 March 1908. The Vienna paper is distinct from the later Bolshevik Pravda; the pool notes the distinction but does not date the transfer of the name, so the relation is stated loosely here.
stops.campa: He settles in Vienna and stays seven years, the longest he lives anywhere between the steppe and Mexico. A second son, Sergei, is born there in 1908. With Adolph Joffe and Matvey Skobelev he edits a Russian-language Pravda, smuggled east across the border, popular with workers and factional with nobody, whose entire programme is that the party should stop splitting. It folds in April 1912, and the Bolsheviks take the name for a paper of their own. He also covers the Balkan Wars for Kievskaya Mysl, reporting the atrocities in flat sentences and without adjectives.
suggested_refs: The Vienna Pravda, 1908-1912, and the Kievskaya Mysl Balkan War dispatches

stops.name: Paris, Nashe Slovo and the antiwar daily
stops.date_confidence: attested: departure from Vienna for Switzerland on 3 August 1914, arrival in France as a war correspondent on 19 November 1914, editorship of Nashe Slovo from January 1915, deportation from France to Spain in September 1916. Canonical atlas Paris pin (48.8566, 2.3522) inherited. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: War closes Austria to a Russian subject. He leaves Vienna for Switzerland on the third of August 1914 and reaches Paris in November as a correspondent. From January he edits Nashe Slovo, an antiwar daily printed in a language its host country cannot read, arguing that the Entente and the Central Powers are one imperial machine seen from two ends, and that the socialist parties which voted the war credits have destroyed themselves. Almost nobody in socialist Europe agrees with him yet. In September 1915 he crosses back into Switzerland for a conference at Zimmerwald.
suggested_refs: Nashe Slovo, Paris, 1915-1916, the antiwar Russian-language daily he edited

stops.name: Zimmerwald, the manifesto of the antiwar socialists
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Zimmerwald Conference of September 1915 and Trotsky's drafting of its manifesto, staking a position between Lenin's call to turn the war into civil war and the pacifist formulas. The remark about fitting the internationalists of the world into four coaches is his own and widely quoted but not verbatim from a source fetched for this file. Coordinates corrected to 46.883 N, 7.467 E; the pool as supplied gave 46.8608/7.5136, about four kilometres southeast of the village. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Thirty-eight delegates from eleven countries are driven up into the hills above Bern in a few hired coaches, a fact Trotsky notes afterwards with the observation that the internationalists of the world now fit into four of them. In a village inn the socialist movement, having voted a year earlier for its own governments' war budgets, tries to reassemble itself. He drafts the manifesto. It condemns the war, calls for a peace without annexations or indemnities, and declines to call, as Lenin wants, for turning the imperialist war into civil war.
suggested_refs: The Zimmerwald Manifesto, September 1915, drafted by Trotsky

stops.name: Madrid, moved on by a third government
stops.date_confidence: attested: deportation from France to Spain in September 1916 and from Spain to the United States on 25 December 1916, with a Spanish detention in between. The specific prison and the route to the port of embarkation are given in the dossier but were not independently confirmed and are omitted here. Month set to November 1916 for ordering.
stops.campa: France puts him over the Spanish border under police escort. Spain does not want him either. He is detained in Madrid, released, moved to the coast, and on the twenty-fifth of December 1916 put aboard a ship for New York with Natalia and the two boys. Fourteen years after the hay cart the pattern of the life has set: a frontier, a paper, an official, a further frontier. The chapter he will one day write about it is called The Planet Without a Visa, and the title is not a figure of speech. It is an itinerary.
suggested_refs: Trotsky, My Life (1930), Chapter XLV, 'The Planet Without a Visa'

stops.name: The Bronx, 1522 Vyse Avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival in New York on 13 January 1917, residence in the Bronx, writing for the emigre daily Novy Mir, contact with Nikolai Bukharin and Alexandra Kollontai, departure 27 March 1917. The description of the apartment's fittings comes from Trotsky's own account. Later conspiracy claims that Wall Street financed his return find no support in the record.
stops.campa: The family takes a flat at 1522 Vyse Avenue with an elevator, a telephone, a rubbish chute and electric light, none of which they have had in Europe, and the boys are astonished by all four. He writes for the emigre daily Novy Mir, meets Bukharin and Kollontai, speaks in halls to Russian and Jewish workers, and studies American capitalism at close range with the interest of a man examining a machine he expects to outlive. He is in New York ten weeks. The story that Wall Street paid for his passage home is a later invention and there is nothing in the record under it.
suggested_refs: Novy Mir, New York, the emigre daily he wrote for in January to March 1917

stops.name: Halifax, taken off the Kristianiafjord
stops.date_confidence: attested: departure from New York aboard the SS Kristianiafjord on 27 March 1917, removal from the ship by British naval authorities and detention at the Halifax Citadel on 3 April 1917, with the family not interned but lodged in a Halifax hotel and required to report daily to police. The pool as supplied gave a single date, 29 April 1917, conflating the removal with the release; the two are separated here.
stops.campa: The February Revolution has happened and he sails for it on the twenty-seventh of March aboard the Kristianiafjord, a Russian subject going home to a Russia with no Tsar. British naval control officers board at Halifax and take him off the ship on the third of April. Natalia and the two boys are put in a hotel in the town and made to present themselves at the police station every day. He is charged with nothing. The reasoning, where any is offered, is that a revolutionary returning to Petrograd would be a danger to the Allied war effort.
suggested_refs: The Halifax Citadel, where he was first held on 3 April 1917

stops.name: Amherst, a month among German prisoners of war
stops.date_confidence: attested: internment at Amherst, Nova Scotia, for about a month and release on 29 April 1917 under Russian and British diplomatic pressure, including from the Petrograd Soviet and the Provisional Government. The disused foundry building, the number of German prisoners and the ban on his addressing them come from his own account and from standard treatments of the camp. Coordinates corrected to 45.819105 N, 64.210772 W; the pool as supplied gave 45.8331/-64.2036, about 1.6 kilometres off.
stops.campa: He is held four weeks in a disused iron foundry at Amherst alongside German prisoners of war, in a building with no partitions and the foundry smell still in the brick. He lectures the prisoners on the Russian revolution and they listen to him; the camp commandant eventually forbids it, on the complaint of the German officers rather than of the Canadian guards. On the twenty-ninth of April the British let him go, under pressure from the Petrograd Soviet and from the Provisional Government he is going home to overthrow, and he resumes the voyage.
suggested_refs: Amherst Internment Camp, Nova Scotia, and Trotsky's own account of the four weeks there

stops.name: Petrograd, the Interdistrict Group
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival in Petrograd on 17 May 1917 and adherence to the Mezhraiontsy, the Interdistrict Group, which shortly merged with the Bolsheviks. The July Days arrest and his election to the Bolshevik Central Committee at the Sixth Congress are standard in the literature but are not in the verified pool as supplied; flagged as outside the verified set.
stops.campa: He reaches Petrograd in May, two months behind Lenin, and does not join the Bolsheviks. He joins the Mezhraiontsy, the Interdistrict Group, a few thousand social democrats who since 1913 have refused both factions on the grounds he refused them himself. In July the group merges with the Bolsheviks entire and he enters their leadership. Fourteen years of being the man who would not choose a side end inside two months. He spends part of the interval in a Petrograd prison again, arrested in the reaction after the July demonstrations, which is where he is when the party he has just joined is driven underground.
suggested_refs: The Mezhraiontsy (Interdistrict Group) and its merger with the Bolsheviks at the Sixth Congress, July-August 1917

stops.name: Smolny, the Military Revolutionary Committee
stops.date_confidence: attested: election as chairman of the Petrograd Soviet on 8 October 1917 and direction of the Military Revolutionary Committee in the seizure of power on 24 to 25 October Old Style, 6 to 7 November New Style. The date given here is New Style. Coordinates corrected to 59.9464 N, 30.3964 E; the pool as supplied gave 59.9506, about 470 metres north of the building.
stops.campa: On the eighth of October he is elected chairman of the Petrograd Soviet, the office he held for fifty days twelve years earlier. From the Smolny Institute, a school for daughters of the nobility turned into the headquarters of the Soviet, he runs the Military Revolutionary Committee, a body constituted to defend the capital against a German advance and used instead to take it. On the night of the twenty-fourth of October its detachments occupy the bridges, the telegraph, the telephone exchange and the railway stations. The government falls with almost no one killed.
suggested_refs: The Smolny Institute, Petrograd, headquarters of the Soviet and the Military Revolutionary Committee

stops.name: Brest-Litovsk, neither war nor peace
stops.date_confidence: attested: People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs from 8 November 1917, publication of the secret treaties of the imperial government, leadership of the Soviet delegation at Brest-Litovsk from December 1917 to February 1918, the 'neither war nor peace' formula, and his resignation when Lenin's harsher terms prevailed. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: As People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs he does two things. He publishes the secret treaties of the imperial government, the carve-ups of Asia Minor and Persia agreed between allies who had told their populations they were fighting for law, so that the diplomatic archive of Europe is opened by a man whose stated intention is to abolish diplomacy. Then he goes to a fortress town in German-occupied Poland to negotiate with the high command, and stalls, addressing his speeches past the generals in the room to the workers of Berlin and Vienna. The formula he invents for it is neither war nor peace, and the German army answers by advancing.
suggested_refs: The published texts of the secret treaties of the Russian Empire, released November 1917

segments.name: The Armoured Train and the Commissariat

stops.name: Sviyazhsk, the tribunal on the island
stops.date_confidence: attested that Trotsky's armoured train reached Sviyazhsk in August 1918 and that a tribunal there executed a regimental commander and his commissar for unauthorised retreat, under his threatened-death order. The scale of any literal decimation of the unit is contested and is not resolved here. Coordinates corrected to 55.7703 N, 48.6528 E; the pool as supplied gave 55.7833/48.9833, about twenty-one kilometres east of the island. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Czechoslovak Legion holds Kazan and the Red units in front of it are dissolving. He arrives on an armoured train fitted with a telegraph office, a printing press, a garage of cars, a library and a staff, and he stops the retreat with a method argued about ever since: a tribunal on the island, and the shooting of a regimental commander and his commissar for pulling back without orders. He also brings boots, pay, hot food and a newspaper printed on board that night. Both halves are the method. The Red Army is being made here, in August, out of almost nothing.
stops.quote: But I am ready to recognize that civil war is no school of humanism.
stops.quote_source: Hue and Cry Over Kronstadt (1938), written in Coyoacan
suggested_refs: Trotsky's armoured train, its press and telegraph, and the Sviyazhsk tribunal of August 1918
sources: Trotsky, Hue and Cry Over Kronstadt (1938), marxists.org

stops.name: Tsaritsyn, the quarrel with Stalin
stops.date_confidence: attested that Trotsky and Stalin clashed bitterly over command at Tsaritsyn in 1918 and that Stalin later inflated the episode while the rewritten civil war histories minimised Trotsky's role. The renaming of Tsaritsyn to Stalingrad in 1925 is general knowledge and is not in the verified pool as supplied. Month set to October 1918 for ordering.
stops.campa: On the lower Volga the local command is in the hands of Joseph Stalin, who is shooting military specialists, that is, former imperial officers, on suspicion, and disregarding orders from the Commissariat of War on principle. Trotsky demands his recall and gets it. The quarrel is about whether an army can be built out of professionals whose politics you distrust. Trotsky wins it. Seven years later the city is renamed Stalingrad, and the histories of the civil war are rewritten afterwards, with Trotsky's part in them shrinking each time.
stops.quote: The dictatorship of the proletariat, in its very essence, signifies the immediate supremacy of the revolutionary vanguard, which relies upon the heavy masses, and, where necessary, obliges the backward tail to dress by the head.
suggested_refs: The Tsaritsyn command dispute of 1918 and its later treatment in Soviet civil war historiography

stops.name: The Kremlin, the Commissariat of War
stops.date_confidence: attested: People's Commissar for Military and Naval Affairs from 14 March 1918 to January 1925, and a Red Army of roughly 5.5 million by late 1920. The month is set to November 1920 to sit at the figure quoted for the army's peak strength.
stops.campa: He is People's Commissar for Military and Naval Affairs for nearly seven years. In that time scattered Red Guard detachments become an army of some five and a half million, officered in large part by former imperial officers recruited as military specialists over ferocious objection from inside his own party, and held to their duty by commissars attached at every level of command. He writes in these same years about the coming body of communist man while ordering the present one shot for desertion. Both texts are his, written within four years of each other.
stops.quote: Man will become immeasurably stronger, wiser and subtler; his body will become more harmonized, his movements more rhythmic.
stops.quote_source: Literature and Revolution (1924), Chapter 8, 'Revolutionary and Socialist Art'
suggested_refs: Trotsky, Terrorism and Communism (1920) and Literature and Revolution (1924), written within four years of each other

stops.name: The Kremlin, the answer for Kronstadt
stops.date_confidence: the Kronstadt rising of March 1921 and its suppression are attested generally; the verified pool contains Trotsky's 1938 statement of responsibility but supplies no geography for Kronstadt itself. This stop therefore sits at the Kremlin, seat of the government that ordered the suppression, and not at Kronstadt, where Trotsky was not personally present. The quoted sentence is from 1938, seventeen years later, and is dated in its own source line. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The sailors of the Kronstadt garrison, who had been the shock troops of October, rise against the government of October, demanding soviets without Bolsheviks, free speech for workers and peasants, and an end to grain requisitioning. The rising is put down across the ice of the gulf with heavy losses on both sides and reprisals afterwards. Trotsky does not command the assault in person and never once denies the decision behind it. Seventeen years later, in Mexico, with the charge coming at him from anarchists, liberals and Stalinists at the same time, he sets down in print exactly what he will and will not answer for.
stops.quote: I was a member of the government, I considered the quelling of the rebellion necessary and therefore bear responsibility for the suppression.
suggested_refs: Trotsky, Hue and Cry Over Kronstadt (1938), his own defence of the 1921 suppression
sources: Trotsky, Hue and Cry Over Kronstadt (1938), marxists.org

stops.name: Moscow, expelled from the party
stops.date_confidence: attested: expulsion from the Communist Party in 1927 following opposition demonstrations tied to the United Opposition with Zinoviev and Kamenev. The verified pool gives only the year; the demonstrations of 7 November 1927 and the expulsion of 14 November are standard datings outside the verified set, so the stop is dated 1927-01-01 for ordering.
stops.campa: Lenin has been dead three years. The Left Opposition has argued and lost on the pace of industrialisation, on party democracy, on the Chinese revolution, and on the whole question of whether socialism can be finished inside one country. On the tenth anniversary of the revolution its supporters march in Moscow and Leningrad with banners of their own and are beaten off the streets by organised squads. Trotsky and Zinoviev are expelled from the party in November. He is forty-eight.
suggested_refs: The Platform of the United Opposition (1927) and the demonstrations of 7 November 1927

stops.name: Alma-Ata, the year inside the union
stops.date_confidence: attested: internal exile to Alma-Ata in Soviet Kazakhstan from January 1928 to January 1929, with correspondence to Oppositionists, analysis of Comintern defeats, hunting, and refusal to recant. The specific counts of letters and telegrams come from Trotsky's own record of the year and are not independently confirmed here. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Deported to Kazakhstan, four thousand kilometres from Moscow, he sets up in a house at the foot of the Tian Shan and works as though the desk were still in the Kremlin. Over the year he sends out hundreds of letters and telegrams to Oppositionists scattered across other places of exile and receives about as many back, until the post is cut. He hunts in the autumn. He writes the analyses of the Chinese defeat and the Comintern programme that are among the sharpest things he ever produced. The GPU asks whether he will undertake to abstain from political activity. He will not.
suggested_refs: Trotsky's Alma-Ata correspondence with the Left Opposition, 1928, and The Third International After Lenin

stops.name: Odessa port, put aboard ship
stops.date_confidence: attested: deportation from the Soviet Union in February 1929, embarking at Odessa for Turkey. The refusals of entry by other European governments are standard in the literature and are not in the verified pool as supplied; flagged. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: They put him on a steamer at Odessa in February with Natalia and their elder son, and take him out into the Black Sea. He is fifty. He has been in this port as a schoolboy in a Lutheran classroom, as a prisoner in a transit cell, and as a fugitive with a false name in his pocket, and now he is cargo. No government in western Europe will have him. Turkey takes him because Turkey is the only one asked that says yes. The ship sails in February and he never sees Russia again.
suggested_refs: The February 1929 deportation order removing Trotsky from Soviet territory

stops.name: Istanbul, stateless
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival in Turkey in February 1929 as a stateless political refugee, first lodging in Istanbul before the move to Buyukada, and publication of My Life by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1930 with translations into German, French, Italian and Polish in the same period. That the first lodging was the Soviet consulate is standard in the literature but is not in the verified pool; flagged. Day set to the fifteenth for ordering only.
stops.campa: He lands as a stateless man holding a Soviet passport that has been cancelled behind him, and is lodged first in the city, at the Soviet consulate of all addresses, before the household is moved out to one of the islands in the Sea of Marmara. He is writing the autobiography. Its last chapter is about the visa, about the discovery that a man can be refused entry by every government on a planet whose surface is entirely claimed by governments. He finishes it in 1929. Scribner's publishes it in New York the following year, and it goes into German, French, Italian and Polish within months.
stops.quote: Despite their slight savor of ecclesiastical eloquence, those are fine words. I subscribe to them.
stops.quote_source: My Life: An Attempt at an Autobiography (1930), closing line of Chapter XLV, 'The Planet Without a Visa'
suggested_refs: My Life: An Attempt at an Autobiography, Charles Scribner's Sons, New York, 1930
sources: Trotsky, My Life (1930), Chapter XLV, marxists.org

stops.name: Buyukada, the History written on an island
stops.date_confidence: attested: residence on Buyukada (Prinkipo) from 1929 to 1933 and composition there of My Life and the three-volume History of the Russian Revolution. The 1931 fire that damaged part of the residence is a dossier claim that could not be independently confirmed in this pass; whether it was accident or arson was never conclusively resolved, and it is carried here as [R]. Fishing with a local boatman comes from Trotsky's own account. Dated 1930-01-01 for ordering.
stops.campa: On Prinkipo, largest of the Princes' Islands, the household takes a decaying villa above the water and turns it into a small international office: secretaries, guards, a mailbag arriving from four continents, and the beginnings of an opposition that has no state behind it anywhere. He fishes with a local boatman most mornings before work. In four years he writes the History of the Russian Revolution, three volumes on an event whose decisive week he organised himself, a book his political enemies concede is great. In 1931 fire damages part of the house. Accident and arson are both alleged and nothing is ever established.
stops.quote: The privilege of historic backwardness – and such a privilege exists – permits, or rather compels, the adoption of whatever is ready
stops.quote_source: History of the Russian Revolution (1930-32), Volume I, Chapter 1, 'Peculiarities of Russia's Development', translated by Max Eastman
suggested_refs: The History of the Russian Revolution, three volumes, written on Buyukada 1930-1932
sources: Trotsky, History of the Russian Revolution, marxists.org

stops.name: Royan, France under guard
stops.date_confidence: attested: admission to France in 1933 under restrictive conditions and residence under close surveillance, at Royan on the Atlantic and later near Barbizon. The alias under which he lived and the later move to the Isere are standard in the literature and are not in the verified pool as supplied; flagged. Month set to July 1933 for ordering.
stops.campa: France admits him on conditions: no Paris, no public meetings, no publicity, a fixed address, and a police guard which is also a police watch. He lives at Royan on the Atlantic coast, then in a house near Barbizon, then further inland, moved on each time a local newspaper works out who the foreigner behind the shutters is. From these rented rooms he tells the German left, with an urgency almost nobody else reaches, that Hitler is not a passing episode, that the Communist line of treating social democrats as the main enemy is suicide, and that a united front is the only instrument left. He is not listened to.
suggested_refs: Trotsky's writings on Germany, 1930-1933, including What Next? and The Only Road

stops.name: Wexhall near Honefoss, dictating The Revolution Betrayed
stops.date_confidence: attested: Norwegian asylum from 1935, residence with the family of the socialist editor Konrad Knudsen at Wexhall near Honefoss, and the composition there of The Revolution Betrayed. The diary entry quoted is verified in the Harvard edition of Diary in Exile (1958, translated by Elena Zarudnaya), dated 8 May 1935; Marxists.org does not host the diary, which is why every path tried there returns 404. Month set to June 1935 for ordering; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Norway admits him and he stays at Wexhall, the house of Konrad Knudsen, a Labour Party editor and member of parliament, in farm country north of Oslo. He is fifty-five and ill for much of the year. He dictates The Revolution Betrayed: the argument that the Soviet Union is neither socialist nor capitalist but a workers' state captured by a privileged bureaucracy, which no reform will dislodge and only a political revolution will. It is the last full book he completes. He also keeps a diary that year in which the politics keeps giving way to other subjects, most of them unpolitical.
stops.quote: Old age is the most unexpected of all the things that happen to a man.
stops.quote_source: Diary in Exile, 1935, entry of 8 May 1935 (Harvard University Press, 1958, translated by Elena Zarudnaya)
suggested_refs: The Revolution Betrayed (1936), dictated at the Knudsen house; Diary in Exile, 1935
sources: Trotsky, Diary in Exile, 1935 (Harvard University Press, 1958)

stops.name: Hurum, interned by a Labour government
stops.date_confidence: attested: the break-in at the Norderhov house by Nasjonal Samling members on 5 August 1936, the internment ordered by Justice Minister Trygve Lie on 2 September 1936 at a farm at Hurum some sixty kilometres from Oslo, house arrest with correspondence restricted, and deportation on 19 December 1936. The pool as supplied placed the internment at Oslo; Oslo was the seat of the government that ordered it, not the site, and the stop is re-placed here. Hurum coordinates are approximate. The content of the Moscow trial testimony is general knowledge and is not in the verified pool.
stops.campa: On the fifth of August members of the Norwegian fascist party break into the Knudsen house and go through his papers. Three weeks later the first Moscow trial opens and Zinoviev and Kamenev confess in open court to conspiring with Trotsky. Under Soviet diplomatic and trade pressure the Labour government of Norway answers by interning the man whose papers were stolen: on the second of September the Minister of Justice, Trygve Lie, has Trotsky and Sedova moved to a farm at Hurum and held under house arrest with their correspondence stopped, unable to answer a word of the trial in public. They are there until December.
suggested_refs: The internment order of 2 September 1936 and the Hurum house arrest, Storsand/Sundby

stops.name: Tampico, the tanker Ruth
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival at Tampico aboard the oil tanker Ruth on 9 January 1937, asylum granted by President Lazaro Cardenas on the intervention of Diego Rivera and Mexican leftists, and a presidential train sent to bring the party to the capital. That Rivera was ill and that Frida Kahlo met the ship in his place is standard in the Kahlo literature and in this corpus's Kahlo material, and is not itemised in the verified pool as supplied.
stops.campa: The oil tanker Ruth docks at Tampico in the second week of January. Lazaro Cardenas has granted asylum, on the petition of Diego Rivera and the Mexican left, and has sent his own presidential train down to the port to carry the passengers inland. Trotsky at first refuses to come off the ship until he sees a face on the quay that someone he trusts has vouched for. Frida Kahlo is on the quay, standing in for Rivera, who is ill. He has never met her. She walks him down the gangway, and they go north to Mexico City on the presidential train.
suggested_refs: The Mexican asylum decree of 1937 and the presidential train sent to Tampico

stops.name: Casa Azul, Coyoacan: the Blue House and the Dewey Commission
stops.date_confidence: attested: residence at the Casa Azul on Londres from January 1937 to April 1939, the Dewey Commission hearings held there in April 1937 and their finding of not proven, and the affair between Trotsky and Frida Kahlo inside the arrangement. Canonical atlas Casa Azul pin inherited byte-identical: 19.3551, -99.1624. The count of sessions and hours of testimony is standard in accounts of the hearings and is not itemised in the verified pool. Dated to the April hearings.
stops.campa: Rivera and Kahlo give over the Blue House on Londres, the house Kahlo was born in, and the Trotskys live in it for two years and three months. In April a commission of inquiry chaired by the American philosopher John Dewey sits in the dining room for thirteen sessions, with the windows sandbagged, and Trotsky answers in English for days to charges he has never been permitted to answer in a Soviet court. The commission finds the Moscow trial accusations not proven. In the same house and the same months he begins an affair with Kahlo, conducted partly in English so that Natalia Sedova will not follow it.
suggested_refs: The Case of Leon Trotsky (1937), the verbatim record of the Dewey Commission hearings at the Casa Azul

stops.name: Coyoacan, the manifesto written with Breton
stops.date_confidence: attested in the corpus's Breton material and in the standard literature: Breton in Mexico in 1938, taken in by Rivera and Kahlo, and the joint drafting with Trotsky of 'Pour un art revolutionnaire independant', published over the signatures of Breton and Rivera although Trotsky wrote much of it. Canonical atlas pin for the Trotsky house inherited byte-identical from the Breton file: 19.3577, -99.1595. Note the geography and afterlife lenses of the research pool give 19.3578, -99.1596 for the same building, a difference of about fifteen metres; the canonical atlas pin is used for consistency. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Andre Breton comes to Mexico and is taken in by Rivera and Kahlo, and he and Trotsky write together a manifesto for an independent revolutionary art. They travel, argue, and draft; Trotsky writes much of the final text and then keeps his name off it, because a manifesto for the freedom of art should not carry the signature of a politician. It goes out over the names of Breton and Rivera. Its position is that art serves the revolution by refusing to take orders from it, and that the freedom it asks for is complete.
suggested_refs: 'Pour un art revolutionnaire independant' (1938), signed by Breton and Rivera, largely drafted by Trotsky

stops.name: Avenida Viena 19, the house behind the river
stops.date_confidence: attested: the rupture with Rivera, the move in April 1939 to the rented house on Avenida Viena, now Avenida Rio Churubusco 410 in Colonia del Carmen, and the household of secretaries and volunteer guards. The heavy fortification (watchtowers, steel doors, bricked windows) is attested as following the May 1940 raid, so it is placed at that stop and not here. The Fourth International was founded at Perigny near Paris in September 1938 on a programme Trotsky wrote in Mexico; he did not attend and no stop is placed at Perigny. Month set to May 1939 for ordering.
stops.campa: The break with Rivera is political and personal and total, and in April 1939 the household moves four streets to a rented house on Avenida Viena, backing onto the Churubusco river. The September before, a conference outside Paris that he could not attend, because no government on earth would give him the papers to travel, had founded the Fourth International on a programme he wrote at this desk. In the new house he keeps rabbits and chickens in the yard, grows cactus he collects himself out in the hills, dictates to secretaries, and works from before dawn. He is sixty. The guard is a handful of young volunteers.
stops.quote: A means can be justified only by its end. But the end in its turn needs to be justified.
suggested_refs: The Transitional Programme (1938), written in Mexico for the founding congress of the Fourth International
sources: Trotsky, Their Morals and Ours (1938), marxists.org

stops.name: Avenida Viena 19, the machine guns before dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested: the raid of 24 May 1940 led by the muralist David Alfaro Siqueiros with the NKVD operative Iosif Grigulevich, the survival of Trotsky and Sedova by taking cover, the wounding of the grandson Vsevolod 'Sieva' Volkov (shot in the foot) and the murder of the guard Robert Sheldon Harte. The number of raiders, the round count and the exact hour are standard details not itemised in the verified pool. The fortification of the compound followed this attack.
stops.campa: Before dawn a party of men in police and army uniform overpower the guard on the gate, walk into the courtyard and empty machine guns into the bedroom wall for several minutes. Trotsky and Sedova get off the bed onto the floor in the corner and are not hit. The grandson, Sieva, aged fourteen, is shot in the foot. The party is led by the muralist David Alfaro Siqueiros, who had commanded a battalion in Spain, working with the NKVD officer Iosif Grigulevich. The guard Robert Sheldon Harte is taken away with them and is found dead a month later. After this come the watchtowers and the steel doors.
suggested_refs: The bullet holes still visible in the walls of the Museo Casa de Leon Trotsky, Coyoacan
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Museo Casa de Leon Trotsky'

stops.name: Avenida Viena 19, the study
stops.date_confidence: attested: Ramon Mercader's alias Frank Jacson, the shortened Austrian piolet made by Werkgen Fulpmes concealed under a raincoat, the pretext of an article he wanted read, the blow to the skull, and penetration of about seven centimetres into the brain. The two-year cultivation of a woman in the Trotsky circle and the number of prior visits to the house are standard in the literature and are not itemised in the verified pool. The murder weapon is a mountaineering ice axe with a pick and a flat adze, not an ice pick; the popular term is a later misnomer that historians and the museum reject.
stops.campa: Ramon Mercader has spent two years becoming Frank Jacson, a Belgian businessman, by way of a courtship of a woman inside the Trotsky circle. He has been in the house several times and the guards no longer search him. On the afternoon of the twentieth of August he brings an article he wants read and keeps his raincoat on in the Mexican summer. Trotsky sits at the desk with the manuscript. Mercader takes from under the coat an Austrian mountaineering axe with the shaft cut down by half and strikes once, with the flat adze, at the back of the skull. The blade goes seven centimetres into the brain. Trotsky does not fall. He shouts, and he fights.
suggested_refs: The ice axe itself, removed from Mexican police evidence by officer Alfredo Salas, sold in 2005 by his daughter to H. Keith Melton, who donated it to the International Spy Museum, Washington DC, where it is displayed; Esteban Volkov publicly doubted its authenticity

stops.name: Cruz Verde, the death the following day
stops.date_confidence: the death on 21 August 1940 from the brain injury is attested, as are the crowds of an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 filing past the coffin between 21 and 27 August, Mercader's conviction and twenty-year sentence in 1943, his term at Lecumberri, his release in 1960 and his later honours in the USSR. The instruction to the guards not to kill his attacker is reported rather than documented and is flagged [R]. The hospital is named as Cruz Verde in the dossier; its exact address could not be independently confirmed and the pin is approximate.
stops.campa: The guards beat Mercader half to death in the study and Trotsky, still conscious, tells them not to kill him, because the man has to talk. He is taken to hospital and operated on through the night, and he dies the following day of the brain injury, the blood loss and the shock, aged sixty. Between two and three hundred thousand people file past the coffin in Mexico City over the following week. Mercader gives a false name and a false motive, is sentenced to twenty years, serves every one of them in Lecumberri, walks out in 1960, and is made a Hero of the Soviet Union.
suggested_refs: The Mexican police file on Jacques Mornard alias Frank Jacson, whose true identity as Ramon Mercader was not established until years later

stops.name: Coyoacan, the stele in the garden
stops.date_confidence: attested: burial of the ashes beneath a stone stele designed by Juan O'Gorman in the garden of the house, with a hammer and sickle and a red flag; the ashes of Natalia Sedova (died 23 January 1962 at Corbeil-Essonnes) and the remains of Esteban Volkov (born 7 March 1926 at Yalta, died 16 June 2023 in Mexico City) were later placed in the same stone. The house was declared a historical monument on 24 September 1982 and opened as the Museo Casa de Leon Trotsky on 20 or 21 August 1990, English and Spanish sources differing by one day. Canonical atlas pin inherited byte-identical; the geography and afterlife lenses of the pool gave 19.3538/-99.1495 and 19.3467/-99.1619 for this same garden, disagreeing with each other and both wrong. Burial date set to late August 1940.
stops.campa: He is cremated and the ashes are buried in the garden of the house, under a plain rectangular stele of stone cut by the architect Juan O'Gorman, with a hammer and sickle in the face of it and a red flag on a pole above. The bullet holes from May are in the wall behind. Natalia Sedova, who dies outside Paris in 1962, is laid in the same stone. So, in 2023, is Sieva, who was shot in the foot at fourteen, who took the name Esteban Volkov, and who kept the house open as a museum for the rest of a life that ran to ninety-seven years.
suggested_refs: The O'Gorman stele in the garden of the Museo Casa de Leon Trotsky, Avenida Rio Churubusco 410, Coyoacan
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Museo Casa de Leon Trotsky'
